deck.name: Web Security
deck.description: Атаки на веб-приложения и защита от них

cards.definition_en: An attack in which someone gets their own script to run inside a trusted website, so it executes in the browsers of other visitors.
examples: The comment form allowed cross-site scripting because it printed user text without encoding.
A strict content policy limits the damage of cross-site scripting.
common_mistakes: Abbreviating it as CSS: the usual abbreviation is XSS, because CSS already means style sheets.
Thinking it only affects the server: the script runs in the visitor's browser.

cards.definition_en: A flaw where text typed by a user ends up inside a database command and changes what that command does.
examples: Parameterized queries remove the risk of SQL injection in the login form.
The audit found an SQL injection in the search page.
common_mistakes: Saying 'SQL inject' as a noun: use 'SQL injection' for the flaw and 'inject' only as a verb.
Believing that escaping quotes by hand is as safe as parameterized queries.

cards.definition_en: An attack that makes a logged-in user's browser send an unwanted request to a site that trusts the user's cookies.
examples: A hidden form on another page triggered cross-site request forgery and changed the user's email.
The framework adds an anti-token to stop cross-site request forgery.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with cross-site scripting: here the attacker does not run code on your site.
Writing 'forgary' instead of 'forgery'.

cards.definition_en: A trick where a page is hidden under or inside another page so that a visitor clicks something different from what they think.
examples: Forbidding framing of the site is the standard defense against clickjacking.
The attacker used clickjacking to make users press a hidden 'Delete account' button.
common_mistakes: Spelling it as 'click jacking' or 'clickjaking'.
Treating it as a bug in the user's mouse or browser instead of a design flaw of the page.

cards.definition_en: Cleaning data from untrusted sources by removing or neutralizing the parts that could be harmful.
examples: Sanitization of the comment field removes script tags before saving.
Relying only on sanitization is risky; encode the output as well.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym of validation: validation rejects bad data, sanitization changes it.
Confusing it with disinfecting hardware; here it concerns data.

cards.definition_en: Checking that the data a program receives has the expected type, length and format before using it.
examples: Input validation rejected a phone number with letters in it.
Client-side checks are not enough, so the server repeats the input validation.
common_mistakes: Thinking that checking in the browser is enough.
Calling it 'inputs validating' instead of using the noun phrase.

cards.definition_en: A browser mechanism that lets a server say which other websites are allowed to read its responses.
examples: Without cross-origin resource sharing headers the browser blocks the script from reading the API reply.
A wildcard in the cross-origin resource sharing settings let any site call the endpoint.
common_mistakes: Believing it protects the server from requests: it only controls what scripts in the browser may read.
Treating it as the same thing as the same-origin policy: it is the controlled way to relax that policy.

cards.definition_en: A browser rule that stops a script loaded from one site from reading data that belongs to another site.
examples: The same-origin policy prevents a random page from reading your bank's data.
Two addresses with different ports count as different origins under the same-origin policy.
common_mistakes: Assuming an origin is only the domain name: it also includes the scheme and the port.
Thinking the policy blocks sending requests, when it mainly blocks reading the replies.

cards.definition_en: A response header that tells the browser which sources of scripts, images and other content a page may use.
examples: A strict content security policy blocks inline scripts that an attacker injects.
We tested the content security policy in report-only mode first.
common_mistakes: Thinking it replaces input validation: it only reduces the damage of injected code.
Writing 'contents security policy'.

cards.definition_en: An attack in which the attacker makes a victim use a session identifier the attacker already knows, and then uses it after the victim logs in.
examples: Issuing a new session identifier after login stops session fixation.
The report described session fixation through an identifier placed in the address.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with session hijacking: in fixation the attacker chooses the identifier, in hijacking they steal it.
Believing that HTTPS alone prevents it.

cards.definition_en: Taking over a user's active session by stealing its identifier and then acting as that user.
examples: Marking the cookie as HttpOnly makes session hijacking through scripts harder.
Session hijacking on public Wi-Fi was easy before sites moved to HTTPS.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with session fixation.
Writing 'highjacking' instead of 'hijacking'.

cards.definition_en: A flaw that lets an attacker use sequences like '../' in a path to reach files outside the folder the application meant to expose.
examples: The download script was open to directory traversal and returned the password file.
Normalizing the path before opening the file blocks directory traversal.
common_mistakes: Using 'travel' instead of 'traversal'.
Thinking it needs special privileges: it works when the program does not check the path.

cards.definition_en: A filter in front of a website that reads incoming web requests and blocks the ones that look like attacks.
examples: The web application firewall blocked thousands of injection attempts last night.
A web application firewall helps, but it does not replace fixing the code.
common_mistakes: Treating it as the same as a network firewall: it understands web requests, not only addresses and ports.
Thinking it makes an insecure application safe.

cards.definition_en: Restricting how many requests one client may send in a given period of time.
examples: Rate limiting on the login page slows down password guessing.
The service answers with an error when rate limiting is triggered.
common_mistakes: Writing 'rating limiting'.
Counting only requests per user and forgetting limits per address.

cards.definition_en: A small challenge that a person can solve easily but an automated program usually cannot.
examples: The sign-up form shows a CAPTCHA after several failed attempts.
Some CAPTCHA challenges are hard to use for people with poor eyesight.
common_mistakes: Writing it in lower case as an ordinary word.
Thinking a CAPTCHA stops all bots: determined attackers use solving services.

cards.definition_en: A header with which a site tells browsers to use only encrypted connections to it for a stated period of time.
examples: After enabling HSTS the browser upgrades every request to HTTPS by itself.
Adding the domain to the HSTS preload list protects even the first visit.
common_mistakes: Expecting HSTS to work on the very first visit without preloading.
Mixing it up with HTTPS: HSTS only enforces its use.

cards.definition_en: A flaw where a site sends visitors to any address given in a request parameter, which attackers use to make harmful links look trustworthy.
collocations: open redirect in the login page
examples: The phishing link used an open redirect on the company's own domain.
Allowing only a list of known paths removes the open redirect.
common_mistakes: Calling every redirect an open redirect: only redirects to unchecked, user-supplied targets are a flaw.
Underestimating it as harmless because no data is stolen directly.

cards.definition_en: An attack that tricks a server into sending requests to addresses chosen by the attacker, often reaching internal systems.
collocations: server-side request forgery in the image fetcher
examples: The image import feature allowed server-side request forgery against the metadata service.
An allow-list of destinations is the best defense against server-side request forgery.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with cross-site request forgery: here the server, not the browser, sends the request.
Forgetting that internal addresses are also targets.

cards.definition_en: A weakness that appears when a program rebuilds objects from data it received without checking that the data is safe.
examples: Insecure deserialization let the attacker run code on the server.
Signing the serialized data helps to detect insecure deserialization attempts.
common_mistakes: Mixing up serialization (writing objects) and deserialization (reading them back).
Trusting data only because it came from the user's own browser.

cards.definition_en: A flaw where an application copies every field from a request into an object, so a user can set fields they should not control.
examples: Mass assignment let a normal user send an extra field and become an administrator.
Listing the allowed fields explicitly prevents mass assignment.
common_mistakes: Thinking it means assigning many tasks to many users.
Binding the whole request body to the model without a whitelist.

cards.definition_en: A weakness caused by unsafe settings, such as default passwords, debug mode left on or storage that anyone can read.
examples: A security misconfiguration left the database open to the whole internet.
Automated checks catch many cases of security misconfiguration before release.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'misconfiguraton' or writing 'miss-configuration'.
Calling it a software bug: the code can be fine while the settings are unsafe.

cards.definition_en: An authorized, simulated attack on a system carried out to find weaknesses before real attackers do.
examples: The company hires specialists for penetration testing every year.
The penetration testing report listed three serious findings.
common_mistakes: Using it for any hacking: it needs written permission from the owner.
Writing 'penetrating testing'.

cards.definition_en: A program in which an organization pays outside researchers for reporting real security problems in its products.
examples: The company paid a large reward through its bug bounty for a serious flaw.
A clear scope is important in every bug bounty.
common_mistakes: Thinking any report is paid: only valid issues inside the rules are rewarded.
Confusing it with penetration testing, which is hired and agreed in advance.

cards.definition_en: The part of an attack that performs the harmful action, or in general the actual data carried by a message.
examples: The email delivered a payload that installed a remote access tool.
The web application firewall inspects the payload of every request.
common_mistakes: Using it only for rockets or trucks: in security it means the harmful part of an attack.
Mixing it up with the whole message or packet, which also has headers.

cards.definition_en: A small piece of data that a website asks the browser to store and send back with later requests, often to recognize a logged-in user.
examples: The server sets a session cookie after the user logs in.
A cookie marked HttpOnly cannot be read by page scripts.
common_mistakes: Thinking a cookie is a program: it is only data.
Storing sensitive details in a cookie without protection.
